response.text:
The Carpet-Bag.

I stuffed a shirt or two into my old carpet-bag, tucked it under my arm, and started for Cape Horn and the Pacific. Quitting the good city of old Manhatto, I duly arrived in New Bedford. It was a Saturday night in December. Much was I disappointed upon learning that the little packet for Nantucket had already sailed, and that no way of reaching that place would offer till the following Monday.

As most young candidates for the pains and penalties of whaling stop at this same New Bedford to embark, it may as well be related that I, for one, had no idea of so doing. My mind was made up to sail in no other than a Nantucket craft, because there was a fine, boisterous something about everything connected with that famous old island which amazingly pleased me. Though New Bedford has of late been gradually monopolising the business, yet Nantucket was her great original—the Tyre of this Carthage. Thence, say they, did those aboriginal whalemen, the Red-Men, first sally in canoes after the Leviathan; and thence the first adventurous little sloop put forth, partly laden with imported cobblestones—so goes the story—to throw at the whales, to learn when they were nigh enough to risk a harpoon from the bowsprit.

Having a night, a day, and still another night before me in New Bedford ere I could embark, it concerned me where to eat and sleep. A dark and dismal night—bitingly cold and cheerless. I knew no one. With anxious grapnels I sounded my pocket and only brought up a few pieces of silver.—Wherever you go, Ishmael, said I to myself, shouldering my bag in the middle of a dreary street, wherever in your wisdom you may conclude to lodge for the night, my dear Ishmael, be sure to inquire the price, and don’t be too particular.

With halting steps I paced the streets, and passed “The Crossed Harpoons.” Further on, from the red windows of the “Sword-Fish Inn” came such a glare that it seemed to have melted the packed snow and ice from before the house. Too expensive and jolly, again; so on, waterward, where, doubtless, were the cheapest, if not the cheeriest inns.

Such dreary streets! blocks of blackness on either hand, and here and there a candle, like a candle moving about in a tomb. Presently a smoky light from a low, wide building, its door invitingly open. Entering, I stumbled over an ash-box in the porch. “The Crossed Harpoons,” and “The Sword-Fish?”—this, then, must be the sign of “The Trap.” However, hearing a loud voice within, I pushed on and opened an interior door.

It seemed the great Black Parliament sitting in Tophet. A hundred black faces turned to peer; beyond, a black Angel of Doom was beating a book in a pulpit. It was a negro church; and the preacher’s text was about the blackness of darkness, and the weeping and wailing and teeth-gnashing there. Ha, Ishmael, muttered I, backing out,—Wretched entertainment at the sign of “The Trap!”

Moving on, I came to a dim light not far from the docks, and heard a forlorn creaking; looking up, saw a swinging sign faintly representing a tall jet of misty spray, and these words underneath—“The Spouter Inn:—Peter Coffin.” Coffin?—Spouter?—Rather ominous in that particular connexion. Yet the place looked quiet and poor enough: a dilapidated little wooden house, as if carted from the ruins of some burnt district; the sign with a poverty-stricken creak. Here, thought I, the very spot for cheap lodgings.

A queer place—a gable-ended old house, one side palsied and leaning sadly, on a sharp bleak corner, where that tempestuous wind Euroclydon kept up a worse howling than ever it did about poor Paul’s tossed craft. Euroclydon, nevertheless, is a mighty pleasant zephyr to any one in-doors, with his feet on the hob quietly toasting for bed. “In judging of that tempestuous wind called Euroclydon,” says an old writer—“it maketh a marvellous difference, whether thou lookest out at it from a glass window where the frost is all on the outside, or whether thou observest it from that sashless window, where the frost is on both sides, and of which the wight Death is the only glazier.” True enough—old black-letter, thou reasonest well. Yes, these eyes are windows, and this body my house. What a pity they didn’t stop up the chinks and crannies; but it’s too late now. The universe is finished; the copestone is on, and the chips were carted off a million years ago. Poor Lazarus there, chattering his teeth against the curbstone, he might plug both ears with rags and yet not keep out Euroclydon. Euroclydon! says old Dives, in his red silken wrapper—pooh, pooh! What a fine frosty night; how Orion glitters; what northern lights! Let them prate of oriental summer climes; give me the privilege of making my own summer with my own coals. But what thinks Lazarus? Would he not rather be in Sumatra than here? go down to the fiery pit itself to keep out this frost? Now, that Lazarus should lie stranded there on the curbstone before the door of Dives, this is more wonderful than that an iceberg should be moored to one of the Moluccas. Yet Dives too lives like a Czar in an ice palace made of frozen sighs; and, being a president of a temperance society, he only drinks the tepid tears of orphans.

But no more of this blubbering now, we are going a-whaling, and there is plenty of that yet to come. Let us scrape the ice from our frosted feet, and see what sort of a place this “Spouter” may be.
